procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad dated 08.02.2023 in CRLA Nos. 5033, 5100 and 5102 of 2019, granting bail to Arvind Kumar, Chandra Kumar @ Chandu, and Rishi Kumar.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Arvind Kumar, Chandra Kumar @ Chandu, and Rishi Kumar filed separate Criminal Appeals (CRLA Nos. 5033, 5100, and 5102 of 2019) before the Allahabad High Court against the Sessions Court order dated 06.06.2019, which convicted them under Sections 147, 148, 302/149, and 120B of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced them to life imprisonment. They sought suspension of sentence and bail, arguing they had been in jail for over ten years and that two co-accused had already been granted bail. The High Court granted them bail during the pendency of their appeals.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Complainant (Appellant) challenged the High Court's order granting bail to Arvind Kumar, Chandra Kumar @ Chandu, and Rishi Kumar in the Supreme Court via Special Leave Petitions (SLP(Crl.) Nos. 7961-7963 of 2023), which were converted into Criminal Appeals No. 2170-2172 of 2024. The Appellant argued that the applicants are "dreaded criminals" and that their release on bail could endanger the complainant and his family. The Appellant contended that the High Court's decision to grant bail was made without considering all relevant facts, particularly the applicants’ subsequent criminal conduct and the ongoing.

decision.appeal_result: The appeal against Arvind Kumar is dismissed, and other two appeals i.e. against Chandra Kumar and Rishi Kumar are allowed.
directions: The impugned order of the High Court granting bail to Rishi Kumar and Chandra Kumar is set aside.
They may surrender within two weeks failing which the High court will take appropriate steps for taking them into custody using coercive measures as are permissible under law.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in granting bail to the accused who were also involved in the murder of a police constable.

facts: Two accused, Chandra Kumar and Rishi Kumar, were convicted for a double murder and sentenced to life imprisonment.
While in judicial custody for the initial murder trial, they murdered a police constable, Ajay Kumar, and attempted to escape.
A separate trial is ongoing for the murder of the police constable.
The High Court granted bail to these two accused, as well as to a co-accused, Arvind Kumar.
The High Court's decision was based partly on the principle of parity, as two other co-accused in the original murder case had already been granted bail.
law: When deciding on bail, a court must consider all relevant facts, including the subsequent criminal conduct of the accused.
The principle of parity (treating co-accused similarly) is not applicable when the roles and subsequent actions of the accused are clearly distinguishable.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court had not been made aware of the crucial fact that Chandra Kumar and Rishi Kumar had murdered a police constable while in custody.
This subsequent, grave crime was a highly relevant fact that should have been considered in the bail application.
The Court determined that the principle of parity did not apply because the other co-accused who received bail were not involved in the constable's murder.
The subsequent violent conduct of Chandra Kumar and Rishi Kumar disentitled them to bail, despite their long period of incarceration.
However, since the other co-accused, Arvind Kumar, was not involved in the murder of the constable, the Court did not interfere with the bail granted to him.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court was not justified in granting bail to Chandra Kumar and Rishi Kumar because it failed to consider their subsequent and serious crime of murdering a police constable. Consequently, the Supreme Court cancelled their bail.

issue.issue_text: Whether the bail granted to the co-accused, who was not a party to the murder of the police constable, warrants interference.

facts: The High Court granted bail to three co-accused: Arvind Kumar, Chandra Kumar, and Rishi Kumar.
Two of the co-accused, Chandra Kumar and Rishi Kumar, murdered a police constable, Ajay Kumar, while in judicial custody.
The co-accused in question, Arvind Kumar, was not charge-sheeted or involved in the murder of the police constable.
law: An accused's eligibility for bail is assessed based on their individual role and conduct.
The principle of parity does not apply when the circumstances and subsequent criminal conduct of co-accused are distinctly different.
application: The Supreme Court differentiated Arvind Kumar's case from that of the other two co-accused, Chandra Kumar and Rishi Kumar.
The Court noted that the primary reason for cancelling the bail of Chandra and Rishi Kumar was their subsequent and serious crime of murdering a police constable.
Since Arvind Kumar was not a party to this subsequent murder, the Court found that the grounds for cancelling the other co-accused's bail did not apply to him.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided not to interfere with the bail granted to the co-accused, Arvind Kumar, because he was not involved in the separate crime of murdering the police constable, unlike the other co-accused whose bail was cancelled for that specific reason.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in granting bail to the accused who were also involved in the murder of a police constable.
appellant_arguments: The accused are 'dreaded criminals' who have committed multiple murders, including the murder of a police constable.

The High Court's decision to grant bail was made without considering all relevant facts, particularly the accused's subsequent criminal conduct and the ongoing trial for the murder of the police constable.
The appellant fears that if the accused are released on bail, they may conspire to harm the complainant and his family members.
respondent_arguments: The provided text does not explicitly state the respondents' arguments, but they would have supported the High Court's order granting them bail.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the bail granted to the co-accused, who was not a party to the murder of the police constable, warrants interference.
appellant_arguments: The appellant challenged the common High Court order that granted bail to all the accused, including this co-accused.
respondent_arguments: The case of this co-accused is different from the others as he was not a party to the murder of the police constable.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A court's failure to consider an accused's subsequent and serious criminal conduct, such as a crime committed during the course of a trial, is a valid ground for setting aside an order granting bail.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court differentiated between the co-accused based on their subsequent criminal conduct. The two accused who were also facing a separate trial for the murder of a police constable were not entitled to bail, despite their long incarceration, because of this subsequent conduct. However, the court found no reason to interfere with the bail granted to the third co-accused, as he was not involved in the subsequent murder.
legal_tests_applied: When evaluating the grant of bail, the court will consider the subsequent conduct of the accused, which can be a determinative factor that outweighs others, such as the period of incarceration.
why_appellant_lost: The appeal against accused Arvind Kumar was dismissed because he was not charge-sheeted in the subsequent murder case of the police constable, and as such, the court was not inclined to interfere with the High Court's order granting him bail.
why_respondent_won: Respondent Arvind Kumar's bail was upheld because he was not a party to the subsequent murder of the police constable.

Respondents Chandra Kumar and Rishi Kumar lost their appeal because their 'subsequent conduct for which they are facing separate trial' disentitled them to the grant of bail, despite their period of incarceration of more than 10 years.
